northern-soul.d: American soul 7-inch singles rediscovered in the dancehalls of northern England: fast, hard on the beat, rare — Frank Wilson's record, pressed in tiny numbers, became the holy grail.

southern-soul.d: Soul from the American South: rawer horns, slower grooves and church-style shouting, with Stax and Otis Redding at its core.

deep-soul.d: The slowest, most bitter branch of Southern soul: strings, torn-up voices and heartbreak; James Carr's "The Dark End of the Street" is the specimen.

blue-eyed-soul.d: Soul sung by white artists: Dusty Springfield and the Righteous Brothers proved soul was never a matter of skin colour.

p-funk.d: Parliament-Funkadelic's cosmic funk: synth bass, space-opera concepts and a full band live — funk turned into mythology here.

go-go.d: Washington DC's funk offshoot: congas, call-and-response and a groove that never lets up; Chuck Brown is the godfather.

electro-funk.d: Funk meets synthesizers and drum machines: Zapp's talk box and slow mechanical grooves fed straight into electro and West Coast hip-hop.

minneapolis-sound.d: Prince's own blend of funk, rock and synthesizers — one of the sexiest pop sounds of the 1980s.

latin-jazz.d: Afro-Cuban rhythm married to bebop harmony: Dizzy Gillespie and Chano Pozo's "Manteca" is the starting point.

gypsy-jazz.d: Hot jazz made in Paris by Django Reinhardt and Stéphane Grappelli: acoustic guitar, rapid arpeggios and swing.

west-coast-jazz.d: The California take on cool jazz: polished arrangements, cool-toned timbres and chamber-like restraint — Chet Baker was its face.

soul-jazz.d: Bringing gospel and blues grooves into jazz: Hammond organ, repeating riffs and a dancefloor feel; Jimmy Smith is the exemplar.

jazz-funk.d: Jazz improvisation fused with funk grooves: electric piano, synthesizers and irresistible basslines; Herbie Hancock's "Chameleon" is the anthem.

spiritual-jazz.d: Jazz as religious experience: long tones, free improvisation and African percussion; Pharoah Sanders' "The Creator Has a Master Plan" is scripture.

ethio-jazz.d: Ethiopian pentatonic scales mixed with jazz harmony: Mulatu Astatke set traditional melodies inside Latin and jazz rhythms.

nashville-sound.d: Wrapping country songs in strings and choruses so they could reach pop radio: Patsy Cline's "Crazy" is the perfect specimen.

bakersfield-sound.d: A reaction against Nashville strings: electric guitar, the Telecaster's sharp bite and hard barroom dancefloor rhythms; Buck Owens is the exemplar.

countrypolitan.d: The Nashville Sound upgraded: thicker strings, more urban arrangements; Glen Campbell's "Wichita Lineman" is the peak.

western-swing.d: Country strings plus jazz big band and swing rhythms: Bob Wills' band set fiddles and horns swinging together in the dancehalls.

alt-country.d: Country sung with indie rock's grit and attitude: Uncle Tupelo's "No Depression" gave a whole generation its name.

americana.d: A contemporary tag that stitches country, folk, blues and rock roots back together; Wilco and Gillian Welch both belong to it.

country-pop.d: Country storytelling and voices placed in pop arrangements: Dolly Parton's "Jolene" has both banjo and a chart placing.

bro-country.d: 2010s American radio country: trucks, beer, cut-off shorts and rapped rhythms; Florida Georgia Line are the exemplars.

euro-disco.d: Continental European disco: synthesizers, four-on-the-floor kick and catchy choruses — Boney M sold it to the whole world.

space-disco.d: Disco that uses synthesizers and sequencers to create weightlessness; Giorgio Moroder and Donna Summer's "I Feel Love" practically invented electronic dance music.

blues-rock.d: Chicago blues handed to electric guitar, high volume and rock drums: Cream and Led Zeppelin turned it into stadium sound.

boogie-rock.d: Hard rock built on the boogie bass figure: repetitive, swinging and made for driving; ZZ Top are the Texas standard-bearers.

swamp-rock.d: Louisiana swamp atmosphere, blues and rock stirred together: Creedence's "Born on the Bayou" is the definitive track.

tejano.d: Texas-Mexican music: accordion, synthesizers and pop melodies, which Selena carried across the whole of America.
